notes.meaning: Dan receives the first strip of land along the northern boundary, stretching all the way from east to west. In earlier times, Dan had fallen into idol worship and received its land last, but here God places Dan first by His grace. The territory forms a straight, orderly band across the top of the country.

Asher and Naphtali each receive a full strip of land running from east to west, directly south of Dan. These tribes are placed in the north near where their ancient homelands once lay. Each tribe receives equal access across the full width of the land.

Manasseh and Ephraim, the two tribes descended from Joseph, receive the next two portions side by side. In the past, half of Manasseh lived east of the Jordan River, but here all the tribes dwell together inside the land. Their borders run parallel to one another in neat order.

Reuben and Judah receive the next two portions, stretching from the eastern boundary to the Mediterranean Sea. Reuben was Jacob's firstborn, and Judah was the tribe that stayed faithful to the temple and to David's royal line. Judah is given the place of honor directly beside the sacred central district.

South of Judah lies a special tract of land set apart for the Lord, matching the length of the tribal portions from east to west. The sanctuary of the temple stands right in the center of this district. This placement shows that the worship of God belongs at the very heart of the community.

Within this set-apart district, a section twenty-five thousand units long and ten thousand units wide belongs to the priests. The temple of the Lord stands right in the middle of this area. Surrounding the sanctuary with the homes of the priests keeps the holy place honored and cared for.

This most holy land is given to the priests from the family of Zadok. They stayed true to God when the rest of the nation and the other Levites turned away to worship idols. God rewards faithful leaders who refuse to follow the crowd into sin.

The Levites who assist the priests receive their own section equal in size, running twenty-five thousand units long and ten thousand units wide. They are strictly forbidden to sell, trade, or give away any part of it. Because this land is set apart for the Lord as the best portion, it must stay dedicated to Him forever.

The remaining area, five thousand units wide and twenty-five thousand units long, is set aside for the city, its homes, and open land. It is called common or unholy only because it is used for everyday living rather than temple worship. The city itself sits right in the center of this strip.

The city itself is laid out as an exact square, measuring four thousand five hundred units on every side. Around the city walls is an open strip of pastureland two hundred and fifty units wide in every direction. Together, the city and its open grounds make a balanced square of five thousand units.

The farmland on the east and west of the city supplies food for the people who work in the city. These workers come from all twelve tribes of Israel, not just one tribe. This means the city belongs to the whole nation and serves all God's people equally.

The combined holy district, including the land for the priests, Levites, and city, forms an exact square of twenty-five thousand units on each side. The whole square is dedicated to God as a special offering from the land. Its four-sided shape reflects balance, stability, and God's perfect design.

The rest of the land stretching east to the Jordan and west to the Mediterranean on both sides of the holy district belongs to the prince. This ruler receives his own estate so he will not need to oppress or take land from the people. In the middle of his territory lie the holy district and the sanctuary, nestled safely between Judah and Benjamin.

South of the sacred district, Benjamin, Simeon, and Issachar receive their portions running from east to west. Benjamin is given the choice border next to the sanctuary because of its longtime loyalty to God's house and David's kingdom. Simeon and Issachar follow in order as the allotments continue toward the south.

Zebulun and Gad receive the next parallel strips of territory across the south. Gad, which previously lived on the east side of the Jordan River, is gathered into the main land with all the other tribes. God gives every tribe its rightful place and home.

Gad's southern boundary marks the southern edge of the entire country, running from Tamar to Kadesh and along the Brook of Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea. This boundary matches the outer border given earlier in the prophet's vision. It sets a clear limit for the inheritance of God's people.

The Lord declares that this is the land to be distributed by lot as an inheritance to the tribes of Israel. Every tribe receives a secure and lasting portion by God's own decree. None of God's people are forgotten when He gathers them home.

The vision now turns from the tribal lands to describe the outer walls and exits of the city. The description begins on the north side, which measures four thousand five hundred units long. This introduces the orderly plan for entering and leaving the city.

The city has twelve gates, each named after one of the tribes of Israel. On the north side are the gates of Reuben, Judah, and Levi, while the east side has gates for Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan. Naming the gates after all the tribes shows that every part of God's family has free access to the city.

The south side contains gates named for Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun, while the west side has gates for Gad, Asher, and Naphtali. Each wall measures four thousand five hundred units long and features three gates. This balanced layout welcomes people from every direction into the city.

The total distance around the city walls is eighteen thousand units, and the city receives a new name: 'The Lord is there.' In earlier visions, Ezekiel saw God's glorious presence leave Jerusalem because of the people's sins, but now the Lord returns to stay permanently. The greatest blessing for God's people is knowing that the Lord Himself dwells among them.
